  "guide": "# Designing frames for a Canvas

A frame is an open web page (scripts, CDN libraries and fonts run). Good frames come from a process, not from more CSS:
context, a direction, foundations, then the boards, then a check. This one text is what an AI team with a designing role and every
MCP agent are given (it is the `GUIDE` in `server/services/canvas_design.py`; the skill file in
`.claude/skills/canvas-design/` is generated from it and a test fails if they differ).

**Beside this guide** (the skill's folder; outside Claude Code, docs_read(design_guide) gives `craft` and the examples' path): `craft.md`,
how a design stops looking machine-made (read it before the first frame), and two exemplar boards in `examples/`,
`foundations.png` and `states.png` (each with its `.html`). The exemplars are the bar for how a design is **presented**
(a document, states side by side, captions). They are a work tool's UI: never take their look (green, pills, hairline
cards, the fonts) for another product, which gets its own.

**Other design skills never set the look.** A board run's prompt lists the skills installed for you, each by its exact
name and the work it covers. Colour, type, layout and the signature come from this guide and craft.md, never from a
skill's rule set: a palette derived by rule from one hue, a stock type scale and white cards on a tinted ground left a
live run flat, in one hue. Open a skill with the Skill tool only for a craft this guide does not teach (motion, 3D, a
chart) when you reach that work, or to check boards you have drawn (critique, accessibility, the handoff spec). Where
one disagrees with this guide, the guide wins. The canvas speaks the product's language: board titles, captions and notes are in the
language of its copy.

## 0. Context before anything

Design is rooted in what exists. Before the first line of code, look for the product's own screens (other frames, a
ticket or page that describes it), its brand or design system, its code (components, CSS variables) and screenshots.
Match its vocabulary: tone of the copy, palette, density, radius, shadows, hover and pressed states. Designing a whole
product from nothing is the last resort; if you must, say what you assumed. Where you have no icon or asset, draw a
plain labelled placeholder. To recreate a UI whose source you can read, build from that source (exact paddings, radii,
sizes), not from memory. Do not recreate another company's distinctive proprietary UI; make an original design that does
the same job.

## 1. Ask once, then decide

With a person there to answer (Claude Code can use `AskUserQuestion`), ask **one** round of at most 4 questions before the
first frame, only if two or more result-changing decisions are open (which job the screen does first, who lands on it, what
to reuse or break from, what may be added). Questions come from their material, never a stock form. Each has 2 to 4
concrete options that differ on a named axis, your pick first marked "(Recommended)". Never re-ask a settled point. When
nobody can answer (a headless run, "just make it"): decide, build, and state your assumptions in one line.

## 2. Direction: character before pixels

Name these and keep them for the whole canvas: **purpose and user**, **tone**, **the signature**, and **type, colour,
space**.

- **The signature** is an element only this product would have, which shapes its main screen and still reads at
  thumbnail size: a budget whose month is an envelope that empties, a transit app drawn as its own line map, a
  habit tracker as a chain that gains a link a day. Find this product's own; never reuse an example from this guide.
  A 2 px tick on a progress bar is a detail, not a signature. If the name of the app could be swapped and nothing would
  look wrong, there is no signature yet.
- **Calm is not characterless.** An app used every day carries no decoration (no hero art, no gradient wash, no
  ornament), and it still has a face: a type pairing chosen for this product, a colour that owns the screen, a
  composition, the signature. A landing page, a splash or a poster can go further: a bold display face, a ground with
  depth, a grid-breaking layout.
- **Explore before you build.** For a new product or a new main screen, draw that screen three ways that differ on a
  named axis (the signature, light or dark, density, the type), at full fidelity with the same real data, on a
  "Directions" page. With a person to answer (`AskUserQuestion`, or `ai_run(ask)` in a board run), show them and let
  them choose. Otherwise judge each at thumbnail size against the tells in `craft.md`, keep the strongest, and say why.
  The rest of the canvas follows the chosen one; the choice stays chosen.
- Do not converge on the same choices from one brief to the next. A cream ground, a serif display and terracotta, or a
  white app of rounded cards with one blue, are habits, not directions. Inter, Roboto or the system face as the display
  face is the template look, unless the product already uses it.

## 3. Content

- Real copy, written for this product: real names, amounts, dates, counts, error messages. Never lorem ipsum, never
  filler that could describe any business. A missing fact is a visible placeholder like `[YOUR PRICE]`.
- Every state says what happened and what to do next ("Plan for 4 tickets is waiting for your approval", "Needs you:
  choose a sender address"), never blame and never a bare "Error".
- Every element earns its place: no filler sections, decorative numbers, icons or stats. **Ask before adding** sections,
  pages or copy nobody mentioned.

## 4. Tokens

One `tokens.css` copied into every frame (or one `:root` block), and nothing in a frame that is not a token.

| Token | Rule of thumb |
| --- | --- |
| Neutrals | ink, muted, line, surface, background; tinted slightly toward the brand (never pure grey on pure white) |
| Colour | in `oklch()`: one colour that owns the screen (a ground, a fill, the signature), at most two accents sharing its chroma and lightness; state colours used sparingly, on the thing they concern |
| Spacing | 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, plus one large step for the signature |
| Radius | one family chosen for the tone (sharp 2 to 6, soft 10 to 16, or round), not 8/12/16 by habit |
| Type | 1 to 3 families with the product's language (Vietnamese needs its subset); a display face with character for numbers and titles, a plain body face; a real scale contrast (the hero number 3 to 5 times the body); line height 1.4 text, 1.1 display; `text-wrap: balance` on titles |
| Elevation | group by space and alignment first, a hairline second; a container only for a real separate object |
| Motion | a few staged moments, not micro-animation everywhere; honour `prefers-reduced-motion` |

## 5. Layout and hierarchy

- Mobile first, 8 px grid, 16 to 20 px side gutters; group by proximity. Flex or grid with `gap`, never siblings spaced by
  margins.
- One primary action per screen, in the lower half on a phone; tap targets at least 44 px; no text under 12 px. In every
  state (an alert, an error, a banner) that action stays on the first phone screen (844 px tall).
- The title and the main action are what the eye finds first, by size, weight and colour, not borders around everything.
- A web view differs from the phone on purpose (a second column, a side pane), not a stretched phone. Fluid roots
  (`max-width`, %, rem); a grid of cards is `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(280px, 100%), 1fr))`.
- Diagrams: a flowchart of separate placed elements, not one big `<svg>`; `<svg>` is for an icon, a logo or a chart.

## 6. Built to be used

- Real `<button>`, `<a href>` and `<input>` with a `<label>`, even in a static mockup; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`;
  decorative SVG is `aria-hidden="true"`. Icons are inline SVG with one stroke width (1.75 to 2). Never emoji as icons.
- No fake phone chrome: no painted status bar ("9:41", battery), no fake keyboard; the device draws them.
- Draw the states, not only the happy screen: pressed, selected, disabled, empty (say what to do next), loading, error,
  offline, long text.
- Text contrast at least 4.5:1 (3:1 from 24 px); grey captions and white text on a fill fail most often. Colours told
  apart differ in lightness, not only hue. Never colour alone for a state: add an icon or a word. Visible focus.

## 7. The canvas is a design document

A canvas that designs a product or a feature is read like a document, not browsed like a gallery of screens. (One frame
asked for, or a change to one, stays a frame.)

- **Pages, in order**: Directions (a new product), Wireframes (when asked), Foundations, Components, then one page per
  area of screens ("Screens · Today"), set with `"page"` in `frame.json`. Each page opens with a title label.
- **Wireframes** show structure before style: every screen in greys, real labels, no colour or type choices, side by
  side in the order of the flow, with the steps between them; a caption names what each screen must answer. The main
  element (the signature, a 3D hero) is a grey line silhouette at its true size and place, never a hatched box with a
  label: its shape, what it overlaps, its states as dashed outlines, and its motion as arrows with timing ("↻ 20 s",
  "↑ 1,4 s"). Secondary pictures stay labelled boxes.
- **Every board is a spec board**: a wide page (1440 to 1800 px, `"fit": true`) that opens with a small uppercase eyebrow
  (`FOUNDATIONS`, `SCREEN · V1`), a title and one or two sentences on what it is for and what it decides. Then lettered
  sections (`a. Type scale, spacing, radii`, `c2. The six states of a reminder card`), each with a heading saying what
  it shows and a one-line lead.
- **States side by side**: the states of one thing in one row, each under a short label (`Empty · first day`,
  `On track`, `Behind · after 3 pm`, `Goal met`, `Offline`), drawn at the same size so only the state changes. Never one
  frame per state. A phone screen is a 390 px wide panel inside the board, real markup, not a picture.
- **A caption beside each decision**: one or two muted lines saying the rule and why ("Visual size can be smaller than
  the target. The tappable area never overlaps its neighbour."). The reasoning lives on the canvas, not only in a comment.
- **Foundations first, at full depth**, so a developer could build from that one board. Every value named by its use:
  the type scale as `Card title / 15 / 600 / lh 1.35` under a sample in the real face; spacing as `12 card padding`,
  `16 side gutter`; radii as `12 card, button, input`; touch targets (`44 × 44 minimum`); neutrals and brand colours
  with their job; status colours with their rule ("Dot colour only. The name always sits beside it."); then the base
  components with their states in a row (a button: primary, pressed, secondary, disabled, loading, destructive; an input:
  default, focus, error, disabled).
- **Components** next: each repeated piece (a card, a row, a banner, a sheet) with its states and variants side by side.
- **Screens** last, built only from those foundations and components: the screen in its main state, then a section of
  its states, then the web view at its own width.
- **Motion and illustration**, when asked: inline SVG drawn for this product, and motion shown both running (a looping
  demo or a Play button in the board) and as key frames side by side with their timing and easing (`craft.md`).
- A clickable prototype is extra: only when asked, as a last page of phone-size frames joined by arrows (frames share
  `localStorage`, so one can carry data to the next).

## 8. Avoid

The machine-made look (`craft.md` has each with what to do instead): every block a white rounded card on a tinted ground,
an icon in a pale circle on every row, an alert as a tinted box with an icon, a bold title and a paragraph, a pill with
an icon on every status, a row of equal buttons over four tab icons, a gradient wash, a left accent border, emoji. Also:
lorem ipsum, invented numbers, low density dressed up as calm, text under 12 px, one-off pixel values, a frame per
state, the same look as last time.

## 9. Changing an existing design

A small, targeted change (a word, a colour, one element) changes only that: every other layout, size, colour and word stays
exactly as it is. If a broader change would help, finish what was asked and **suggest** the rest. A redesign or a new
direction is different: then make the substantial changes. Follow the design's own vocabulary when you add to it.

## 10. Check before you send

1. Squint: on each screen, are the title and the main action what you see first?
2. Is every gap, size and colour a token, and is the direction (restrained or bold) the one you named?
3. Do the boards read as a document: pages in order, a title and purpose on each, lettered sections, states side by side
   with labels, a caption by each decision, foundations a developer could build from?
4. Does each screen hold at the width it is for (390 for a phone panel, 1280 and 820 for a web view)? No short label
   broken over two lines, nothing cut off, the main action on the first phone screen in every state.
5. States there, copy real, nothing added that nobody asked for? Does it match what was asked, and nothing else changed?
6. The thumbnail test: shrink the main screen to 120 px wide. Is the signature still there, and would it still look
   right under another app's name? Count the tells from `craft.md`; fix each, then look again.
7. Beside the exemplars: is the presentation at their level of structure and finish?

## 11. Hand it over

New canvas: a folder with one sub-folder per frame (`index.html`, optional `frame.json`), then
`docs_write(canvas_create, owner_kind, owner_id, title, path)`; the owner (a ticket or a Docs page) must exist first. Put the
returned `markdown` line on its own line in that ticket or page (`manage_ticket` or `docs_write(update)`).

- **Order and names**: frames are placed left to right in folder-name order on their page, so name the folders
  `01-foundations`, `02-components`, `10-today`; the number is not part of the shown name.
- **`frame.json`**: `{"name", "page": "Foundations", "size": "phone"|"tablet"|"desktop"|[w, h], "fit": true, "x", "y"}`.
  Frames with the same `page` share a page tab, in the order they first appear. A long board is cut off by a fixed
  height: set `"fit": true` and the editor measures the page once, or give `[w, h]`.
- **`canvas.json` at the top**: `labels` (`{"text", "page", "x", "y", "size"}`, a page's title), `notes` (`{"id",
  "text", "near": "<frame>", "page", "x", "y", "color", "w", "h"}`; a note near a frame sits under it, on its page) and `arrows` (`{"from", "to", "label"}`, a frame
  folder name or a note `id`). A wrong reference is reported before anything is created.
- **A spec per screen** on Docs, for whoever builds it: one page per screen (or a section each on one page) with what it
  is for, a screenshot of each state (`![Today · behind](shots/today-behind.png)`, a file in your working folder), the
  tokens and components it uses, sizes and behaviour, the copy of every state, open questions, and the board it is on.
- **Change to an existing frame**: write the changed files to a folder and `docs_write(canvas_update)` with a
  one-sentence note on the design decision; the board changes at once.
- Leave `canvas_comment`s for open questions, each pinned with `at` (a CSS selector, or `text=Add task`). Give your
  assumptions in one line.

  "craft": "# Craft: from machine-made to designed

The design guide (`SKILL.md`) gives the process. This page is about the look: why a screen reads as made by an AI, and
what a designer does instead. Read it before your first frame, and again when you judge your screenshots.

## Why it looks machine-made

A model reaches for the average of every app it has seen: a light tinted ground, white rounded cards, one blue, pills,
icons in circles, a row of buttons, four tab icons. Each choice is reasonable; together they are a template, and a
viewer recognises the template before reading a word. Beauty comes from decisions the average would not make, taken
for reasons that belong to this product.

## The tells, and what to do instead

| Tell | Instead |
| --- | --- |
| Every block is a white rounded card on a tinted ground | Let most content sit on the ground, grouped by space and alignment. Use a container only for a real separate object (a sheet, a dialog, a draggable item). One surface change on a screen is often enough. |
| An icon in a pale tinted circle at the start of every row | Drop the icon when the word says it, or use the icon alone at text size, in the text colour. Repetition is not structure. |
| An alert as a tinted box with an icon, a bold title and a paragraph | Put the state where it happens: the number turns amber, the bar shows the gap, the row shows "not saved · Retry". A banner only for a state that concerns the whole screen, written as one line. |
| A pill with an icon on every status | One state word, set in type (weight, colour, small caps) beside the thing. A pill only where it is a control or a filter. |
| A row of equal buttons above four tab icons | One main action that looks like the main action (size, place, colour). Secondary actions are smaller or quieter, not the same box in another colour. |
| A progress bar plus a percentage plus a sentence saying the same | Pick the one form that is the product's signature and make it big; drop the repeats. |
| One brand blue on a near-white ground | Let a colour own the screen (a dark ground, a strong fill, the signature in colour) or commit to ink on paper with one sharp accent. |
| Inter, Roboto or the system face everywhere, weights 400 to 600, sizes 14 to 24 | A display face with character for titles and numbers, a plain body face, and real contrast in scale: the hero number three to five times the body size, tight tracking at large sizes. |
| Everything centred, everything the same width | A left edge everyone aligns to, one element that breaks it on purpose, a rhythm of big and small. |
| Generous empty space at the bottom of every phone screen | Size the composition to the content, or give the space to the signature. Empty space is a decision, not leftover. |
| Gradient wash, glassmorphism, drop shadow on every card, emoji, a left accent border | Leave them out. Depth, if the tone wants it, comes from one shadow or one layered element. |

## Character, piece by piece

**Type.** Pair a display face with a plain body face. Choose for the product's voice and its language: Vietnamese needs a
family with the Vietnamese subset (for example Be Vietnam Pro, Bricolage Grotesque, Big Shoulders Display, Fraunces,
Lexend, Baloo 2, Space Grotesk, Archivo, Plus Jakarta Sans, Montserrat, JetBrains Mono, Roboto Mono). Numbers are the
heroes of most apps: give them the display face, tabular figures and size. Small uppercase labels with letter-spacing
are one tool, not the default for every heading.

**Colour.** Build the palette in `oklch()`. Neutrals lean toward the main hue (chroma 0.005 to 0.02). Decide what owns the
screen: a ground, a fill, the signature. Accents share the main colour's chroma and lightness and change the hue.
Colours that must be told apart differ in lightness. Use state colours on the thing they describe, never as five tinted
boxes.

**Composition.** Decide what the eye meets first, second and third, and make the sizes say so: one element clearly the
largest. Align to a few edges. Let the signature take room: bleed to the edge, overlap a boundary, fill the screen if
that is the point. Density is good when it is ordered; an app people check ten times a day wants the answer at once.

**The signature.** Ask what this product is about in the physical world (money leaves an envelope; a train runs
along a line; a habit is a chain you add a link to) and find this product's own, simply drawn, as the main screen's
structure. It must survive at thumbnail size and in every state: empty, on track, behind, done, offline, error.

**Details.** One icon set, one stroke width, sized to the text beside it. Optical alignment of icons and numbers. Real
copy with the product's voice; a state says what happened and what to do. Pressed and focus states drawn.

## Motion and SVG

**Motion earns its place.** Animate what helps people understand a change: something arriving, a value moving toward a
goal, an action confirmed, a state that changed. One staged moment per screen beats many small effects. Entrances ease
out (`cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` or a spring), exits are faster than entrances, UI moves in 150 to 300 ms and a
signature moment in 400 to 900 ms. Animate `transform` and `opacity`, never layout. Nothing loops forever on a working
screen. Everything honours `prefers-reduced-motion` with an instant or a cross-fade version.

**SVG drawn for the product.** Illustration and the signature are inline SVG made for this product, in its palette and
one stroke weight: simple geometric construction, a few shapes, no clip-art people or blobs. An SVG that moves uses
CSS on its parts (`stroke-dashoffset` to draw a line, `transform` on groups) so it stays light and editable.

**Show motion on a canvas.** A screenshot freezes it, so a motion section has two parts: the motion running, and the
key frames side by side (start, middle, end) labelled with duration and easing, so a developer can build it without
guessing. The running demo loops by itself with a pause between plays (a demo that plays once on load has ended
before anyone scrolls to it), and its replay button is a bonus, not the only way to see it.

## Explore, then build

1. Draw the main screen three ways that differ on a named axis (the signature, light or dark, density, type), full
   fidelity, the same real data, on a "Directions" page.
2. Screenshot each at 390 px and look at it at thumbnail size beside the others.
3. Score each against the tells above; check that the signature reads small and in two states (on track, behind).
4. With a person to answer, show them and let them choose. Otherwise keep the strongest, say in one line why, and leave
   the others on the Directions page.
5. Build foundations, components and the screens from the chosen direction only.

## The critique pass

After the screens are built, take screenshots and, for each main screen, write down (for yourself) the three things
that most look like a template. Fix those three, screenshot again, and repeat once. Stop when what remains is a choice
you would defend, not a default you inherited.

- Real `<button>`, `<a href>` and `<input>` with a `<label>`, even in a static mockup; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`;
  decorative SVG is `aria-hidden="true"`. Icons are inline SVG with one stroke width (1.75 to 2). Never emoji as icons.
- No fake phone chrome: no painted status bar ("9:41", battery), no fake keyboard; the device draws them.
- Draw the states, not only the happy screen: pressed, selected, disabled, empty (say what to do next), loading, error,
  offline, long text.
- Text contrast at least 4.5:1 (3:1 from 24 px); grey captions and white text on a fill fail most often. Colours told
  apart differ in lightness, not only hue. Never colour alone for a state: add an icon or a word. Visible focus.

## 7. The canvas is a design document

A canvas that designs a product or a feature is read like a document, not browsed like a gallery of screens. (One frame
asked for, or a change to one, stays a frame.)

- **Pages, in order**: Directions (a new product), Wireframes (when asked), Foundations, Components, then one page per
  area of screens ("Screens · Today"), set with `"page"` in `frame.json`. Each page opens with a title label.
- **Wireframes** show structure before style: every screen in greys, real labels, no colour or type choices, side by
  side in the order of the flow, with the steps between them; a caption names what each screen must answer. The main
  element (the signature, a 3D hero) is a grey line silhouette at its true size and place, never a hatched box with a
  label: its shape, what it overlaps, its states as dashed outlines, and its motion as arrows with timing ("↻ 20 s",
  "↑ 1,4 s"). Secondary pictures stay labelled boxes.
- **Every board is a spec board**: a wide page (1440 to 1800 px, `"fit": true`) that opens with a small uppercase eyebrow
  (`FOUNDATIONS`, `SCREEN · V1`), a title and one or two sentences on what it is for and what it decides. Then lettered
  sections (`a. Type scale, spacing, radii`, `c2. The six states of a reminder card`), each with a heading saying what
  it shows and a one-line lead.
- **States side by side**: the states of one thing in one row, each under a short label (`Empty · first day`,
  `On track`, `Behind · after 3 pm`, `Goal met`, `Offline`), drawn at the same size so only the state changes. Never one
  frame per state. A phone screen is a 390 px wide panel inside the board, real markup, not a picture.
- **A caption beside each decision**: one or two muted lines saying the rule and why ("Visual size can be smaller than
  the target. The tappable area never overlaps its neighbour."). The reasoning lives on the canvas, not only in a comment.
- **Foundations first, at full depth**, so a developer could build from that one board. Every value named by its use:
  the type scale as `Card title / 15 / 600 / lh 1.35` under a sample in the real face; spacing as `12 card padding`,
  `16 side gutter`; radii as `12 card, button, input`; touch targets (`44 × 44 minimum`); neutrals and brand colours
  with their job; status colours with their rule ("Dot colour only. The name always sits beside it."); then the base
  components with their states in a row (a button: primary, pressed, secondary, disabled, loading, destructive; an input:
  default, focus, error, disabled).
- **Components** next: each repeated piece (a card, a row, a banner, a sheet) with its states and variants side by side.
- **Screens** last, built only from those foundations and components: the screen in its main state, then a section of
  its states, then the web view at its own width.
- **Motion and illustration**, when asked: inline SVG drawn for this product, and motion shown both running (a looping
  demo or a Play button in the board) and as key frames side by side with their timing and easing (`craft.md`).
- A clickable prototype is extra: only when asked, as a last page of phone-size frames joined by arrows (frames share
  `localStorage`, so one can carry data to the next).

## 8. Avoid

The machine-made look (`craft.md` has each with what to do instead): every block a white rounded card on a tinted ground,
an icon in a pale circle on every row, an alert as a tinted box with an icon, a bold title and a paragraph, a pill with
an icon on every status, a row of equal buttons over four tab icons, a gradient wash, a left accent border, emoji. Also:
lorem ipsum, invented numbers, low density dressed up as calm, text under 12 px, one-off pixel values, a frame per
state, the same look as last time.

## 9. Changing an existing design

A small, targeted change (a word, a colour, one element) changes only that: every other layout, size, colour and word stays
exactly as it is. If a broader change would help, finish what was asked and **suggest** the rest. A redesign or a new
direction is different: then make the substantial changes. Follow the design's own vocabulary when you add to it.

## 10. Check before you send

1. Squint: on each screen, are the title and the main action what you see first?
2. Is every gap, size and colour a token, and is the direction (restrained or bold) the one you named?
3. Do the boards read as a document: pages in order, a title and purpose on each, lettered sections, states side by side
   with labels, a caption by each decision, foundations a developer could build from?
4. Does each screen hold at the width it is for (390 for a phone panel, 1280 and 820 for a web view)? No short label
   broken over two lines, nothing cut off, the main action on the first phone screen in every state.
5. States there, copy real, nothing added that nobody asked for? Does it match what was asked, and nothing else changed?
6. The thumbnail test: shrink the main screen to 120 px wide. Is the signature still there, and would it still look
   right under another app's name? Count the tells from `craft.md`; fix each, then look again.
7. Beside the exemplars: is the presentation at their level of structure and finish?

## 11. Hand it over

New canvas: a folder with one sub-folder per frame (`index.html`, optional `frame.json`), then
`docs_write(canvas_create, owner_kind, owner_id, title, path)`; the owner (a ticket or a Docs page) must exist first. Put the
returned `markdown` line on its own line in that ticket or page (`manage_ticket` or `docs_write(update)`).

- **Order and names**: frames are placed left to right in folder-name order on their page, so name the folders
  `01-foundations`, `02-components`, `10-today`; the number is not part of the shown name.
- **`frame.json`**: `{"name", "page": "Foundations", "size": "phone"|"tablet"|"desktop"|[w, h], "fit": true, "x", "y"}`.
  Frames with the same `page` share a page tab, in the order they first appear. A long board is cut off by a fixed
  height: set `"fit": true` and the editor measures the page once, or give `[w, h]`.
- **`canvas.json` at the top**: `labels` (`{"text", "page", "x", "y", "size"}`, a page's title), `notes` (`{"id",
  "text", "near": "<frame>", "page", "x", "y", "color", "w", "h"}`; a note near a frame sits under it, on its page) and `arrows` (`{"from", "to", "label"}`, a frame
  folder name or a note `id`). A wrong reference is reported before anything is created.
- **A spec per screen** on Docs, for whoever builds it: one page per screen (or a section each on one page) with what it
  is for, a screenshot of each state (`![Today · behind](shots/today-behind.png)`, a file in your working folder), the
  tokens and components it uses, sizes and behaviour, the copy of every state, open questions, and the board it is on.
- **Change to an existing frame**: write the changed files to a folder and `docs_write(canvas_update)` with a
  one-sentence note on the design decision; the board changes at once.
- Leave `canvas_comment`s for open questions, each pinned with `at` (a CSS selector, or `text=Add task`). Give your
  assumptions in one line.

# Craft: from machine-made to designed

The design guide (`SKILL.md`) gives the process. This page is about the look: why a screen reads as made by an AI, and
what a designer does instead. Read it before your first frame, and again when you judge your screenshots.

## Why it looks machine-made

A model reaches for the average of every app it has seen: a light tinted ground, white rounded cards, one blue, pills,
icons in circles, a row of buttons, four tab icons. Each choice is reasonable; together they are a template, and a
viewer recognises the template before reading a word. Beauty comes from decisions the average would not make, taken
for reasons that belong to this product.

## The tells, and what to do instead

| Tell | Instead |
| --- | --- |
| Every block is a white rounded card on a tinted ground | Let most content sit on the ground, grouped by space and alignment. Use a container only for a real separate object (a sheet, a dialog, a draggable item). One surface change on a screen is often enough. |
| An icon in a pale tinted circle at the start of every row | Drop the icon when the word says it, or use the icon alone at text size, in the text colour. Repetition is not structure. |
| An alert as a tinted box with an icon, a bold title and a paragraph | Put the state where it happens: the number turns amber, the bar shows the gap, the row shows "not saved · Retry". A banner only for a state that concerns the whole screen, written as one line. |
| A pill with an icon on every status | One state word, set in type (weight, colour, small caps) beside the thing. A pill only where it is a control or a filter. |
| A row of equal buttons above four tab icons | One main action that looks like the main action (size, place, colour). Secondary actions are smaller or quieter, not the same box in another colour. |
| A progress bar plus a percentage plus a sentence saying the same | Pick the one form that is the product's signature and make it big; drop the repeats. |
| One brand blue on a near-white ground | Let a colour own the screen (a dark ground, a strong fill, the signature in colour) or commit to ink on paper with one sharp accent. |
| Inter, Roboto or the system face everywhere, weights 400 to 600, sizes 14 to 24 | A display face with character for titles and numbers, a plain body face, and real contrast in scale: the hero number three to five times the body size, tight tracking at large sizes. |
| Everything centred, everything the same width | A left edge everyone aligns to, one element that breaks it on purpose, a rhythm of big and small. |
| Generous empty space at the bottom of every phone screen | Size the composition to the content, or give the space to the signature. Empty space is a decision, not leftover. |
| Gradient wash, glassmorphism, drop shadow on every card, emoji, a left accent border | Leave them out. Depth, if the tone wants it, comes from one shadow or one layered element. |

## Character, piece by piece

**Type.** Pair a display face with a plain body face. Choose for the product's voice and its language: Vietnamese needs a
family with the Vietnamese subset (for example Be Vietnam Pro, Bricolage Grotesque, Big Shoulders Display, Fraunces,
Lexend, Baloo 2, Space Grotesk, Archivo, Plus Jakarta Sans, Montserrat, JetBrains Mono, Roboto Mono). Numbers are the
heroes of most apps: give them the display face, tabular figures and size. Small uppercase labels with letter-spacing
are one tool, not the default for every heading.

**Colour.** Build the palette in `oklch()`. Neutrals lean toward the main hue (chroma 0.005 to 0.02). Decide what owns the
screen: a ground, a fill, the signature. Accents share the main colour's chroma and lightness and change the hue.
Colours that must be told apart differ in lightness. Use state colours on the thing they describe, never as five tinted
boxes.

**Composition.** Decide what the eye meets first, second and third, and make the sizes say so: one element clearly the
largest. Align to a few edges. Let the signature take room: bleed to the edge, overlap a boundary, fill the screen if
that is the point. Density is good when it is ordered; an app people check ten times a day wants the answer at once.

**The signature.** Ask what this product is about in the physical world (money leaves an envelope; a train runs
along a line; a habit is a chain you add a link to) and find this product's own, simply drawn, as the main screen's
structure. It must survive at thumbnail size and in every state: empty, on track, behind, done, offline, error.

**Details.** One icon set, one stroke width, sized to the text beside it. Optical alignment of icons and numbers. Real
copy with the product's voice; a state says what happened and what to do. Pressed and focus states drawn.

## Motion and SVG

**Motion earns its place.** Animate what helps people understand a change: something arriving, a value moving toward a
goal, an action confirmed, a state that changed. One staged moment per screen beats many small effects. Entrances ease
out (`cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1)` or a spring), exits are faster than entrances, UI moves in 150 to 300 ms and a
signature moment in 400 to 900 ms. Animate `transform` and `opacity`, never layout. Nothing loops forever on a working
screen. Everything honours `prefers-reduced-motion` with an instant or a cross-fade version.

**SVG drawn for the product.** Illustration and the signature are inline SVG made for this product, in its palette and
one stroke weight: simple geometric construction, a few shapes, no clip-art people or blobs. An SVG that moves uses
CSS on its parts (`stroke-dashoffset` to draw a line, `transform` on groups) so it stays light and editable.

**Show motion on a canvas.** A screenshot freezes it, so a motion section has two parts: the motion running, and the
key frames side by side (start, middle, end) labelled with duration and easing, so a developer can build it without
guessing. The running demo loops by itself with a pause between plays (a demo that plays once on load has ended
before anyone scrolls to it), and its replay button is a bonus, not the only way to see it.

## Explore, then build

1. Draw the main screen three ways that differ on a named axis (the signature, light or dark, density, type), full
   fidelity, the same real data, on a "Directions" page.
2. Screenshot each at 390 px and look at it at thumbnail size beside the others.
3. Score each against the tells above; check that the signature reads small and in two states (on track, behind).
4. With a person to answer, show them and let them choose. Otherwise keep the strongest, say in one line why, and leave
   the others on the Directions page.
5. Build foundations, components and the screens from the chosen direction only.

## The critique pass

After the screens are built, take screenshots and, for each main screen, write down (for yourself) the three things
that most look like a template. Fix those three, screenshot again, and repeat once. Stop when what remains is a choice
you would defend, not a default you inherited.

{
  "guide": "# Drawing draw.io diagrams

A diagram on this board is a `.drawio` file (XML) that people open in the draw.io editor and change after you. It is
judged by two things: a newcomer understands it in ten seconds, and a person can move one box without the rest falling
apart. This text is what every AI on the board is given (the `DRAWIO` in `server/services/visual_guides.py`, the
`drawio-diagrams` skill; outside Claude Code, `docs_read(action='diagram_guide')`).

## Which tool

| You want to show | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How a screen or page looks: its layout, its states, a click-through | **Canvas** (HTML frames; the `canvas-design` guide) | a real page at real widths, every state side by side |
| Boxes and arrows a team will edit: a user flow's steps and decisions, who does what, a sequence, the states of one thing, the parts of a system, a data model, a plan's dependencies | **draw.io Diagram** in the Docs page or ticket it explains | editable shape by shape, links follow their shapes, one source |
| A person's quick hand drawing, or a mark on a screenshot | **Sketch**, made by a person; you read it (`sketches` guide) | a hand drawing is a person's thinking; yours would be a fake |

- "Draw the sign-up flow and mock up its screens" is two drawings: the flow as a Diagram (steps, decisions, where each
  screen sits), the screens on a Canvas. Link each from the other's page or ticket.
- Draw only when words alone are hard to follow: more than three parts, branches, or an order that matters. A picture
  sits beside the words that explain it, never instead of them; nothing one sentence says needs one.
- A chart of numbers is neither: put it in a Docs page as a table, or as a chart frame on a Canvas.

## 1. One question per diagram

Name the question the diagram answers before you draw ("What happens between Sign up and the first login?"), then pick
the kind that answers it:

| Question | Kind | Shape of it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What are the steps and decisions? | **Flowchart** (a process, a user flow) | one direction, top to bottom or left to right; start and end as pills, steps as boxes, decisions as diamonds |
| Who does which step? | **Swimlane flowchart** | one lane per actor (person, app, server, email), steps in the lane of who does them |
| Who calls whom, in what order? | **Sequence** | lifelines across the top, messages as arrows down the page, in time order |
| What states does one thing go through? | **State machine** | rounded boxes for states, arrows labelled with the event that moves it |
| What are the parts and how do they talk? | **Architecture** (system context, containers) | groups for what is deployed or owned together; arrows labelled with what flows (HTTPS, a queue, a file) |
| What is stored and how is it related? | **Data model** (entity relationship) | one table shape per entity with its key fields; crow's-foot ends for one and many |
| What depends on what? | **Plan / dependency map** | one box per piece of work, arrows for "must come before" |

At most about 25 shapes on a page. More than that is two questions: split into pages (`<diagram>` elements, one per
page) or into an overview and a detail.

## 2. Layout on a grid

- Grid of 10: every `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` is a multiple of 10 (`gridSize="10"` on the `mxGraphModel`).
- **Standard sizes**, so the eye reads rank, not noise: step 160 x 60, decision 120 x 80, start or end 120 x 40,
  data store 120 x 70, note 160 x 60. A label that does not fit makes the box wider in steps of 40, never the text
  smaller.
- **Spacing**: 40 between shapes in a row, 80 between ranks (rows of a top-down flow, columns of a left-right one), 40
  of padding inside a group or lane.
- **The main path is a straight line.** The happy path runs down one axis with its centres aligned; branches leave to
  the side and come back. A loop back (`No` returns to the form) is routed around the outside, never across shapes.
- **Arrows** are orthogonal (`edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle`), enter and leave at the middle of a side, never cross a
  shape and cross each other as little as you can. Fix a crossing by moving shapes, not by adding bends.
- Leave room: a diagram people will extend needs free space beside its last rank.

## 3. Style from one palette

Define the styles once and reuse them by role; never invent a colour for one box. Take the project's own palette when
its other diagrams or design tokens have one (read them first: `docs_read(diagrams)`); otherwise use these:

| Role | Style |
| --- | --- |
| Step (default) | `rounded=1;arcSize=12;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| Decision | `rhombus;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| Start or end | `rounded=1;arcSize=50;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#F1F5F9;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| The focus (what this diagram is about; one or two shapes) | step style with `fillColor=#DBEAFE;strokeColor=#1D4ED8;fontStyle=1;` |
| Error or rejected path | step style with `fillColor=#FEF2F2;strokeColor=#B91C1C;` |
| Outside our system (a person, a third party) | step style with `dashed=1;` |
| Data store | `shape=cylinder3;boundedLbl=1;size=10;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontSize=13;` |
| Group or lane | `swimlane;startSize=30;html=1;fillColor=#F8FAFC;strokeColor=#CBD5E1;fontStyle=1;fontSize=13;` (add `horizontal=0;` for a lane on the left) |
| Note | `shape=note;size=14;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FEF9C3;strokeColor=#CA8A04;fontSize=12;align=left;spacingLeft=8;` |
| Arrow | `edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=1;html=1;endArrow=block;endFill=1;strokeColor=#475569;fontSize=12;fontColor=#334155;` |

- Colour carries one meaning each (the focus, an error path), and never alone: the label says it too. More than one
  coloured meaning gets a small legend in a corner.
- One font size for shapes (13), one for arrows and notes (12), bold only for the focus and group titles. No shadows,
  gradients or 3D.

## 4. Labels

- **Steps are verb phrases** in sentence case ("Send the confirmation email"), things are nouns ("Email service").
  Under six words; the detail goes in the text beside the diagram.
- **Decisions are questions** ("Email already used?") and every exit is labelled (`Yes` / `No`, or the cases).
- **Label an arrow** when it carries something: data, an event, a condition, a protocol. Not "next", not "then".
- The project's language, the product's words: no ticket keys, field names or abbreviations a newcomer would not
  know.
- A title at the top left (a text cell, 16, bold) when the page will be read on its own.

## 5. Groups, containers and lanes

- A shape inside a group has `parent="<group id>"`, and its `x`, `y` are **relative to the group**. Moving the group
  moves everything in it.
- A lane is a group: one per actor, all the same width (top-down) or height (left-right), side by side with no gap.
- Group only what belongs together (deployed together, owned by one team, one step's sub-steps), never just to draw
  a box around things.

## 6. Writing the file

Plain XML, never compressed, with ids that say what they are (`signup-form`, `email-valid`, `e-form-valid`): a
person and the next AI find them, and links stay readable.

```xml
<mxfile><diagram name="Sign-up"><mxGraphModel gridSize="10" grid="1"><root>
  <mxCell id="0"/><mxCell id="1" parent="0"/>
  <mxCell id="landing" value="Open the sign-up page" style="STEP" vertex="1" parent="1">
    <mxGeometry x="40" y="40" width="160" height="60" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
  <mxCell id="email-valid" value="Email valid?" style="DECISION" vertex="1" parent="1">
    <mxGeometry x="60" y="180" width="120" height="80" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
  <mxCell id="e-landing-valid" style="ARROW" edge="1" parent="1" source="landing" target="email-valid">
    <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
</root></mxGraphModel></diagram></mxfile>
```

(`STEP`, `DECISION`, `ARROW` stand for the style strings of section 3.) In a `value`, a line break is `<br>`
and `&`, `<`, `"` are escaped as in any XML attribute. Every link has a `source` and a `target` that are ids of shapes
on the same page. A loop back goes around the outside through bends you give it, on the grid, in page coordinates:
`<mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"><Array as="points"><mxPoint x="540" y="180"/></Array></mxGeometry>`.

**With Flow.** When the Flow skills are open to you (`flow:flowchart`, `flow:sequence`, `flow:er`, `flow:bpmn` and the
other `flow:*`; the board suggests the plugin, github.com/iamcaominhtien/flow), a diagram of a kind it knows is laid
out by it instead of by hand: write its JSON spec, run its `flow.py build`, read its check and fix the spec until the
errors are gone. It writes a `.drawio` in one design (its own palette and sizes, in place of section 3's) and an
`.html` page whose main path moves. Then go on with section 8 on the `.drawio` and hand it in as section 9 says; the
`.html` may go on the ticket as an attachment. A large or dense diagram goes through `flow:author`. Its ids are
`node-<id>` and `edge-<id>`; a later change follows section 7, or `flow:edit-drawio`.

## 7. Changing an existing diagram

People moved those boxes by hand. A change keeps their work:

1. Read it as a model first: `docs_read(action='diagram', diagram_id)` gives every shape and link with its id, label,
   box and style, and the problems it has. Find the cells you will touch by id.
2. Write the file (`docs_read(diagram, diagram_id, path)`) and change **only those cells**: every other id, position,
   size, style and label stays exactly as it is. Never write the whole file again from scratch to change one thing,
   and never rename an id.
3. A new shape takes the style of its neighbours of the same role and a free spot on the grid next to them. Make room
   by moving whole ranks or lanes by 80 or 40, not by nudging single boxes.
4. Save with `docs_write(diagram_save, diagram_id, path, base_version)` and the `version` you read. A stale version is
   refused: read again, redo your change on the new version, save.
5. A bigger change (a new kind, a new layout) is a redesign: say so, and keep the old one in the history (saving makes
   a new version; nothing is lost).

## 8. Look before you hand it in

`docs_read(action='picture', path='<your .drawio>')` (or `diagram_id` for a saved one) writes a PNG: open it and
check, as a newcomer would:

- the main path reads in one direction, in one glance; nothing overlaps; no arrow crosses a shape;
- every label fits its shape, every decision exit is labelled, the words are the product's;
- the colours mean one thing each, and the focus is what you see first.

The save answer lists `problems` (links to nothing, shapes on top of each other) too. Fix, look again.

## 9. Hand it in

- `docs_write(diagram_create, project_id, title, path)` (or `diagram_save`) and put the returned `markdown` line,
  `[Name](diagram:dg_…)`, **on its own line** in the Docs page or ticket the diagram explains, beside the words it
  illustrates. Give it a one-sentence `summary`.
- On the board that line is the picture: it shows the diagram itself, always the latest version. Do not post the
  PNG of `docs_read(picture)` beside it (the same diagram twice); the PNG is for checking (section 8) and for places
  where the line cannot show, such as a pull request. In the ticket's comment, say what the diagram shows in one
  sentence and the open questions.
- A diagram that goes with a design links both ways: the Canvas embed line on the diagram's page or ticket, and the
  diagram's line where the screens are specified.

A Sketch is a freehand drawing a **person** makes on the board: pen strokes on up to 10 layers, often over a
screenshot, stored as a PNG with its layers (`.sketch.json`). It shows in a text as `![Name](sketch:sk_…)`. This text
is what every AI on the board is given (the `SKETCH` in `server/services/visual_guides.py`, the `sketches` skill;
outside Claude Code, `docs_read(action='diagram_guide')`).

## You read Sketches; you do not draw them

A Sketch is worth something because a person drew it while thinking: rough, fast, theirs. Strokes drawn by code give
a fake hand-drawn look that nobody can edit by its parts, and people may take it for a person's idea. Whatever you
want to show is better as a **Diagram** (boxes and arrows anyone can edit) or a **Canvas** frame (the real screen).
So never make a Sketch to draw something, and never save over a person's Sketch.

## Reading one

1. `docs_read(action='sketch', sketch_id, path)` writes its PNG (and its layers): open the PNG and look at it whole.
   `docs_read(action='picture', sketch_id)` gives the PNG alone.
2. Say back what you see in words, in the ticket or page: the parts, their order, what the arrows and marks point at.
   Where a mark could mean two things, ask (one question, your reading first) instead of guessing.
3. Turn it into the right drawing: a screen goes on a Canvas (keep its layout and its words, then design it
   properly), a flow or a structure becomes a draw.io Diagram (keep its parts and their order). Link back to the
   Sketch ("Drawn from ![the sketch](sketch:sk_…)") so the person sees their idea carried over.
4. A comment about the Sketch goes in the ticket or page that shows it; leave the Sketch itself as it is.

# Drawing draw.io diagrams

A diagram on this board is a `.drawio` file (XML) that people open in the draw.io editor and change after you. It is
judged by two things: a newcomer understands it in ten seconds, and a person can move one box without the rest falling
apart. This text is what every AI on the board is given (the `DRAWIO` in `server/services/visual_guides.py`, the
`drawio-diagrams` skill; outside Claude Code, `docs_read(action='diagram_guide')`).

## Which tool

| You want to show | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How a screen or page looks: its layout, its states, a click-through | **Canvas** (HTML frames; the `canvas-design` guide) | a real page at real widths, every state side by side |
| Boxes and arrows a team will edit: a user flow's steps and decisions, who does what, a sequence, the states of one thing, the parts of a system, a data model, a plan's dependencies | **draw.io Diagram** in the Docs page or ticket it explains | editable shape by shape, links follow their shapes, one source |
| A person's quick hand drawing, or a mark on a screenshot | **Sketch**, made by a person; you read it (`sketches` guide) | a hand drawing is a person's thinking; yours would be a fake |

- "Draw the sign-up flow and mock up its screens" is two drawings: the flow as a Diagram (steps, decisions, where each
  screen sits), the screens on a Canvas. Link each from the other's page or ticket.
- Draw only when words alone are hard to follow: more than three parts, branches, or an order that matters. A picture
  sits beside the words that explain it, never instead of them; nothing one sentence says needs one.
- A chart of numbers is neither: put it in a Docs page as a table, or as a chart frame on a Canvas.

## 1. One question per diagram

Name the question the diagram answers before you draw ("What happens between Sign up and the first login?"), then pick
the kind that answers it:

| Question | Kind | Shape of it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What are the steps and decisions? | **Flowchart** (a process, a user flow) | one direction, top to bottom or left to right; start and end as pills, steps as boxes, decisions as diamonds |
| Who does which step? | **Swimlane flowchart** | one lane per actor (person, app, server, email), steps in the lane of who does them |
| Who calls whom, in what order? | **Sequence** | lifelines across the top, messages as arrows down the page, in time order |
| What states does one thing go through? | **State machine** | rounded boxes for states, arrows labelled with the event that moves it |
| What are the parts and how do they talk? | **Architecture** (system context, containers) | groups for what is deployed or owned together; arrows labelled with what flows (HTTPS, a queue, a file) |
| What is stored and how is it related? | **Data model** (entity relationship) | one table shape per entity with its key fields; crow's-foot ends for one and many |
| What depends on what? | **Plan / dependency map** | one box per piece of work, arrows for "must come before" |

At most about 25 shapes on a page. More than that is two questions: split into pages (`<diagram>` elements, one per
page) or into an overview and a detail.

## 2. Layout on a grid

- Grid of 10: every `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` is a multiple of 10 (`gridSize="10"` on the `mxGraphModel`).
- **Standard sizes**, so the eye reads rank, not noise: step 160 x 60, decision 120 x 80, start or end 120 x 40,
  data store 120 x 70, note 160 x 60. A label that does not fit makes the box wider in steps of 40, never the text
  smaller.
- **Spacing**: 40 between shapes in a row, 80 between ranks (rows of a top-down flow, columns of a left-right one), 40
  of padding inside a group or lane.
- **The main path is a straight line.** The happy path runs down one axis with its centres aligned; branches leave to
  the side and come back. A loop back (`No` returns to the form) is routed around the outside, never across shapes.
- **Arrows** are orthogonal (`edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle`), enter and leave at the middle of a side, never cross a
  shape and cross each other as little as you can. Fix a crossing by moving shapes, not by adding bends.
- Leave room: a diagram people will extend needs free space beside its last rank.

## 3. Style from one palette

Define the styles once and reuse them by role; never invent a colour for one box. Take the project's own palette when
its other diagrams or design tokens have one (read them first: `docs_read(diagrams)`); otherwise use these:

| Role | Style |
| --- | --- |
| Step (default) | `rounded=1;arcSize=12;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| Decision | `rhombus;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| Start or end | `rounded=1;arcSize=50;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#F1F5F9;strokeColor=#475569;fontColor=#0F172A;fontSize=13;` |
| The focus (what this diagram is about; one or two shapes) | step style with `fillColor=#DBEAFE;strokeColor=#1D4ED8;fontStyle=1;` |
| Error or rejected path | step style with `fillColor=#FEF2F2;strokeColor=#B91C1C;` |
| Outside our system (a person, a third party) | step style with `dashed=1;` |
| Data store | `shape=cylinder3;boundedLbl=1;size=10;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FFFFFF;strokeColor=#475569;fontSize=13;` |
| Group or lane | `swimlane;startSize=30;html=1;fillColor=#F8FAFC;strokeColor=#CBD5E1;fontStyle=1;fontSize=13;` (add `horizontal=0;` for a lane on the left) |
| Note | `shape=note;size=14;whiteSpace=wrap;html=1;fillColor=#FEF9C3;strokeColor=#CA8A04;fontSize=12;align=left;spacingLeft=8;` |
| Arrow | `edgeStyle=orthogonalEdgeStyle;rounded=1;html=1;endArrow=block;endFill=1;strokeColor=#475569;fontSize=12;fontColor=#334155;` |

- Colour carries one meaning each (the focus, an error path), and never alone: the label says it too. More than one
  coloured meaning gets a small legend in a corner.
- One font size for shapes (13), one for arrows and notes (12), bold only for the focus and group titles. No shadows,
  gradients or 3D.

## 4. Labels

- **Steps are verb phrases** in sentence case ("Send the confirmation email"), things are nouns ("Email service").
  Under six words; the detail goes in the text beside the diagram.
- **Decisions are questions** ("Email already used?") and every exit is labelled (`Yes` / `No`, or the cases).
- **Label an arrow** when it carries something: data, an event, a condition, a protocol. Not "next", not "then".
- The project's language, the product's words: no ticket keys, field names or abbreviations a newcomer would not
  know.
- A title at the top left (a text cell, 16, bold) when the page will be read on its own.

## 5. Groups, containers and lanes

- A shape inside a group has `parent="<group id>"`, and its `x`, `y` are **relative to the group**. Moving the group
  moves everything in it.
- A lane is a group: one per actor, all the same width (top-down) or height (left-right), side by side with no gap.
- Group only what belongs together (deployed together, owned by one team, one step's sub-steps), never just to draw
  a box around things.

## 6. Writing the file

Plain XML, never compressed, with ids that say what they are (`signup-form`, `email-valid`, `e-form-valid`): a
person and the next AI find them, and links stay readable.

```xml
<mxfile><diagram name="Sign-up"><mxGraphModel gridSize="10" grid="1"><root>
  <mxCell id="0"/><mxCell id="1" parent="0"/>
  <mxCell id="landing" value="Open the sign-up page" style="STEP" vertex="1" parent="1">
    <mxGeometry x="40" y="40" width="160" height="60" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
  <mxCell id="email-valid" value="Email valid?" style="DECISION" vertex="1" parent="1">
    <mxGeometry x="60" y="180" width="120" height="80" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
  <mxCell id="e-landing-valid" style="ARROW" edge="1" parent="1" source="landing" target="email-valid">
    <mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"/></mxCell>
</root></mxGraphModel></diagram></mxfile>
```

(`STEP`, `DECISION`, `ARROW` stand for the style strings of section 3.) In a `value`, a line break is `<br>`
and `&`, `<`, `"` are escaped as in any XML attribute. Every link has a `source` and a `target` that are ids of shapes
on the same page. A loop back goes around the outside through bends you give it, on the grid, in page coordinates:
`<mxGeometry relative="1" as="geometry"><Array as="points"><mxPoint x="540" y="180"/></Array></mxGeometry>`.

**With Flow.** When the Flow skills are open to you (`flow:flowchart`, `flow:sequence`, `flow:er`, `flow:bpmn` and the
other `flow:*`; the board suggests the plugin, github.com/iamcaominhtien/flow), a diagram of a kind it knows is laid
out by it instead of by hand: write its JSON spec, run its `flow.py build`, read its check and fix the spec until the
errors are gone. It writes a `.drawio` in one design (its own palette and sizes, in place of section 3's) and an
`.html` page whose main path moves. Then go on with section 8 on the `.drawio` and hand it in as section 9 says; the
`.html` may go on the ticket as an attachment. A large or dense diagram goes through `flow:author`. Its ids are
`node-<id>` and `edge-<id>`; a later change follows section 7, or `flow:edit-drawio`.

## 7. Changing an existing diagram

People moved those boxes by hand. A change keeps their work:

1. Read it as a model first: `docs_read(action='diagram', diagram_id)` gives every shape and link with its id, label,
   box and style, and the problems it has. Find the cells you will touch by id.
2. Write the file (`docs_read(diagram, diagram_id, path)`) and change **only those cells**: every other id, position,
   size, style and label stays exactly as it is. Never write the whole file again from scratch to change one thing,
   and never rename an id.
3. A new shape takes the style of its neighbours of the same role and a free spot on the grid next to them. Make room
   by moving whole ranks or lanes by 80 or 40, not by nudging single boxes.
4. Save with `docs_write(diagram_save, diagram_id, path, base_version)` and the `version` you read. A stale version is
   refused: read again, redo your change on the new version, save.
5. A bigger change (a new kind, a new layout) is a redesign: say so, and keep the old one in the history (saving makes
   a new version; nothing is lost).

## 8. Look before you hand it in

`docs_read(action='picture', path='<your .drawio>')` (or `diagram_id` for a saved one) writes a PNG: open it and
check, as a newcomer would:

- the main path reads in one direction, in one glance; nothing overlaps; no arrow crosses a shape;
- every label fits its shape, every decision exit is labelled, the words are the product's;
- the colours mean one thing each, and the focus is what you see first.

The save answer lists `problems` (links to nothing, shapes on top of each other) too. Fix, look again.

## 9. Hand it in

- `docs_write(diagram_create, project_id, title, path)` (or `diagram_save`) and put the returned `markdown` line,
  `[Name](diagram:dg_…)`, **on its own line** in the Docs page or ticket the diagram explains, beside the words it
  illustrates. Give it a one-sentence `summary`.
- On the board that line is the picture: it shows the diagram itself, always the latest version. Do not post the
  PNG of `docs_read(picture)` beside it (the same diagram twice); the PNG is for checking (section 8) and for places
  where the line cannot show, such as a pull request. In the ticket's comment, say what the diagram shows in one
  sentence and the open questions.
- A diagram that goes with a design links both ways: the Canvas embed line on the diagram's page or ticket, and the
  diagram's line where the screens are specified.

  "guide": "# Working in Docs

Docs is the project's wiki: a tree of Markdown pages beside the board. People read pages in a reading view and edit
them in a rich-text editor; what is stored is Markdown. You read and write the same pages over MCP with `docs_read`
and `docs_write`.

## 1. A page, a ticket comment, or a file?

| It is… | Put it… |
|---|---|
| Something people will come back to after the ticket is done: a spec, a decision and why, how a part works, a how-to, meeting notes | a **page** |
| About this piece of work only: progress, a question, a finding, proof that it works, a hand-over | a **ticket comment** |
| A spec written for a ticket | a **page**, linked to the ticket; the ticket gets one comment that says what the page decides and links it |
| A question about one sentence of a page | an **inline comment** on that sentence (`quote`) |
| Writing for people that is the result of the work (research, a comparison, a spec, a decision, a guide), even when you work in a git folder | a **page**, not a Markdown file in the repository |
| Developer docs that change with the code (a README, the docs the repository keeps beside its code), or a file the ticket asks for | a **file** on the ticket's branch |

Do not paste a page into a comment, or a comment thread into a page. Link instead. A text you already wrote as a file
goes onto a page with `docs_write(action='import')`; then the page is the one people read and change.

## 2. How pages are organised

- `docs_read(action='list', project_id)` is the tree: `parent_id` and `position`. Put a page under the page it
  belongs to (a feature's spec under the feature, an endpoint under API); do not make a new top-level page for each
  ticket.
- Before you create a page, search: `docs_read(action='search', project_id, query)`. Update the page that exists
  instead of starting a second one with the same subject.
- The page **title** is its name in the tree and in links. The body starts at `##` headings; never repeat the title as
  a `#` heading in the body.
- A page you create is published as v1. Every change is a new version with a note; people see who changed what in
  the history, so write a short, true `note`.

## 3. Read before you write

- `docs_read(action='get', page_id)` returns `markdown`, `version`, `headings`, `referenced_by` (pages and tickets that
  link to it) and `work` (the tickets tied to the page and what the AI on each is doing now).
- For one part of a long page: `docs_read(action='get', page_id, section='Endpoints')`.
- A ticket's pages: `get_ticket` lists them under `docs` (its spec, its design notes). Read the ones that matter
  before you work on the ticket.

## 4. Edit a part, not the page

A person may be editing another part of the page while you work. Change only what you mean to change:

- **One section**: `docs_write(action='edit', page_id, section='Endpoints', markdown=..., base_version=<version you
  read>)`. `markdown` replaces the section's body; the heading stays (start `markdown` with a heading of the same level
  to rename it). The section includes its sub-sections.
  - `mode='append'` adds at the end of the section, `prepend` just under its heading, `after` / `before` adds a new
    block (a new `## Section`) after or before it.
  - If that section changed since `base_version`, the edit is refused and the answer shows the section as it is now:
    apply your change to that text and retry. A change elsewhere on the page does not stop you.
- **One passage**: `docs_write(action='edit', page_id, find='exact text from the page', markdown='new text')`. `find`
  must be on the page exactly once (copy it from `get`; add a few words around it if it is not unique). If it is
  gone, someone changed it: read again.
- **Several changes**: `items=[{section|find, markdown, mode}, ...]`: applied in order, published as one version, all
  or nothing.
- **Add to the end**: `mode='append'` with no section.
- `update` (the whole page) is for a page you are writing from scratch or rewriting on purpose, not to fix one line:
  you send the whole page back, and any line you copied wrong changes too.
- `publish=false` keeps your change as your own draft that nobody sees; publish when it is ready. An `edit` works on
  the published text, so publish a draft (`update` with the whole text) before you edit that page.
- **From a file**: `docs_write(action='import', project_id, path)` turns a Markdown file (or a folder, as a tree) into
  published pages. Write the page there when it is long; then link the ticket to it.
- **Read it back**: after you write a page, `docs_read(get)` it once and check the headings and tables are there
  before you tell anyone it is done.

## 5. The Markdown the editor keeps

Write exactly these forms. They render in the reading view and survive a person's edit in the editor unchanged.

| What | Write | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Section headings | `## Section`, `### Sub-section` | Body headings start at `##`. Each heading is a link target (`[[Page#Section]]`) and an entry in "On this page". |
| Bold, italic, strike | `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `~~gone~~` | No underline (`<u>` is dropped). |
| Highlight | `==the key sentence==` | A yellow marker over text, for the one thing a reader must not miss. Use it rarely. |
| Inline code | `` `GET /tickets` `` | Names, paths, commands, values. |
| Links | `[text](https://…)` | A bare URL becomes a link too. |
| Link to a page | `[[Page]]`, `[[Page#Section]]`, `[[Page|shown text]]` | Shown as a chip; the page lists you under "Referenced by". `docs_read(action='check_links', refs=[...])` says whether they resolve. A page that is renamed keeps its links (they are rewritten). |
| Link to a ticket | `KAN-12` (the key, as it is) | Shown as a chip with the ticket's status; the ticket lists the page under its docs. Not inside code. |
| Lists | `- item`, `1. item` | Nest with two spaces. |
| Task list | `- [ ] open`, `- [x] done` | A person ticks them in the reading view. An open item with no ticket key can become a ticket (section 8). |
| Table | `\| Method \| Path \|` / `\|---\|---\|` / rows | GitHub tables, one line per row, `\|` escaped in cells. No cell spans, no blocks in a cell. |
| Code block | ```` ```python ```` … ```` ``` ```` | Name the language: it is coloured. |
| Callout | `> [!INFO]`, `> [!WARNING]`, `> [!SUCCESS]` then `> text` lines | A coloured box: info (a note), warning (a risk, something not done yet), success (a confirmation). `NOTE`, `TIP`, `CAUTION`, `IMPORTANT` are read as one of these three. |
| Quote | `> quoted text` | |
| Picture | `![what it shows](/uploads/…)`, width: `![what it shows|640](/uploads/…)` | Upload it first (section 6). Alt text says what the picture shows. |
| File | `[report.pdf](/uploads/…)` | Shown as a file card that opens in the preview. |
| Diagram, sketch, canvas | `[Name](diagram:dg_…)`, `![Name](sketch:sk_…)`, `![Name](canvas:cv_…)` | On a line of their own, as `diagram_create`, `sketch_create`, `canvas_create` return them. `docs_read(action='diagram_guide')` says which one fits. |
| Math | `$x^2$`, `$$ … $$` | |
| Divider | `---` on its own line | |

Mentions: `@Name` notifies a member **in a comment**, not in a page body (a page's `@Name` is plain text). Raw HTML
is removed. A heading with only a link, an emoji in every heading or a table used for layout reads as machine-made:
write plain sentences under clear headings, short paragraphs, one idea each.

## 6. Pictures and files

- `docs_write(action='upload', path='/abs/file.png', page_id=…)` stores the file and puts it on the page: a picture
  inline, any other file as a file card. Without `section`/`find` it goes at the end; `section='Login'` puts it at the
  end of that section; `find='exact sentence'` puts it in a paragraph of its own after that sentence.
- Your files are not on the board's machine? Send them as `data` (base64) with `name`.
- `ticket_id=KAN-12` (with `body`) posts the file on the ticket as a comment as well; for a ticket alone,
  `ticket_items(item='attachment', path=...)` does the same (the file then shows in the ticket's Attachments).
- Without `page_id` or `ticket_id` it only stores the file and returns `markdown` to put where you want.
- In a board AI run, a picture in your working folder can also be named by its path in the Markdown you send
  (`![Login](qa/shots/login.png)`): the board copies it.

## 7. Comments

- **On a passage**: `docs_write(action='comment', page_id, body, quote='exact text of the page')`. The quote is plain
  text inside one paragraph, list item or table cell. The person sees it highlighted with your comment beside it.
  Make one point per comment; say what is wrong and what you propose.
- **On the page**: omit `quote`.
- **Answer**: `docs_read(action='comments', page_id, state='open')`, then `docs_write(action='reply', thread_id,
  body)`. Read the whole thread first; answer the last question asked.
- Resolve a thread only when its last word asks for nothing, and always reply first: a thread you opened that is now
  answered, a person's thread where they agreed or understood, a requested change you fully made (say where: section,
  version). Leave it open, say what is missing and `@mention` the person when the change is partial, it is a matter of
  taste or a disagreement, or you asked them something; never close a thread the person reopened. The skill
  `docs-comment-threads` (or `docs_read(action='guides')` outside Claude Code) has the rules and the reasons.
- A person can send you a page's threads from Docs ("Send to AI"): the note says so, lists each thread (fenced as data)
  and the skill says how to work them.
- A person who writes `@AI member` in a thread gets an answer there from the page's assistant (when the project has
  Docs AI on). A comment by an AI never wakes another AI (no loops); to tell a ticket's team something, use
  `ai_run(action='message', to='<TICKET-KEY>', text)` inside a run.

## 8. Pages and tickets, both ways

- **Link** a page and a ticket: write the key on the page (`KAN-12`), or `[[Page]]` in the ticket, or
  `manage_ticket(action='link_doc', ticket_id, page_id)`. Do one; both sides then show the link. Read `get_ticket().docs`
  first: a page that is already there (named by the ticket or naming it) is linked, and `link_doc` on it answers
  "already linked" and adds nothing. Link by hand only a page the text does not name.
- **A spec for a ticket**: write the page under the feature's page, put the ticket key in it where the work is
  described, link it, and comment on the ticket: "The spec is [[Login — spec]]: what it decides in one line." The Dev
  on the ticket sees it in `get_ticket().docs` and in its run's prompt.
- **From a checklist to tickets**: `docs_write(action='tickets', page_id)` turns the open task items and action items
  (all, or those in `find`) into tickets, links them and puts each key on its line. Or pass your own drafts in
  `items=[{title, text, type, status, assignee}]`.
- **Give a page to an AI member**: `docs_write(action='assign', page_id, member_id, kind='write'|'review', body=what
  you want)`. It makes the ticket "Write/Review the page “X”", linked and assigned, and starts the member's run. The
  page shows who is working on it and what they are doing; `docs_read(get).work` too.
- A ticket's AI reads its linked pages; the Docs AI reads the tickets a page links when it answers about the page.

## 9. Before you hand in

- Read your page back with `docs_read(action='get')`: headings in order, every `[[link]]` and ticket key resolves
  (`check_links`), tables have the same number of cells in every row, pictures have alt text.
- Say on the ticket what you wrote, with the link, and what is still open.
"
}

  or nothing.
- **Add to the end**: `mode='append'` with no section.
- `update` (the whole page) is for a page you are writing from scratch or rewriting on purpose, not to fix one line:
  you send the whole page back, and any line you copied wrong changes too.

  criterion against it, and fix what you would send back yourself.

A person opens the ticket, not your run. When you finish, the ticket itself must show what happened:

  "evidence-and-handover": "# Evidence and handing over

People and the next AI judge your work by what they can see on the ticket, not by your summary.

## Show it
- **Something a person will look at** (a screen, a page, a canvas): a screenshot of it, taken by you, in a ticket
  comment: `![What it shows](path/in/your/folder.png)`. One picture per state that matters.
- **Code**: the command you ran and its real output in a ``` block (the test run, the build), and the branch or PR
  link. A failing run first and a passing one after, when you fixed a bug.
- **Docs, diagrams, canvases**: the embed line (`![Name](canvas:cv_…)`, `[Name](diagram:dg_…)`, `[[Page]]`) so it opens
  from the ticket, and a picture of it: `docs_read(action='picture')` draws a PNG of a diagram or a frame, to look at
  before you hand in, and returns the `markdown` line that shows it in a comment.
- **Never invent evidence.** A screenshot of something else, output you did not get, or a "should work" is worse than
  saying it could not be shown.

## Hand it over
A role (a subagent) answers the lead with what it found or did, concretely: files, commands, results, and what is
left. The lead's final report (the JSON the run asks for) does the same for the ticket's people: status, summary,
branch, tests, open items. Write either so the reader can act without reading the whole run.

Example:
- Done: the Today screen in 6 states and the components board.
- Where: canvas "Giọt" (pages Foundations, Components, Today); the spec per screen on Docs › Design › Today.
- Left: the web view, not started (the run's budget ran out).
- Check: tokens are in `tokens.css`, use them and do not copy hex values; whether reminders pause in meetings is open
  (asked in a comment).

When you start, read what earlier runs left: the ticket's comments, its work log and what they link (the spec, the
canvas, the branch), before anything else.

## Close the ticket's story
End with one comment that a person reads first: what you handed in (with the pictures), what is left, and what
waits for whom. In a board run the lead's final report is that comment: put the files in it (attach each with
`post=false`, link the markdown it returns) rather than a comment per file and a report on top. What waits for a person says so, by name: "The canvas on Foundations waits for your answer to my comment".

  "repo-and-machine": "# The repository and the machine

## Git
- **Work on the ticket's branch** (or the worktree the board gave you). Never commit to the default branch, and never
  rewrite history that others have: no force-push, no amend of pushed commits.
- **Small commits that say why**: one change each, a message that a reviewer understands without the diff.
- **Run the project's own checks before you hand in** (its test, lint and build commands, in your prompt or the
  README). Report their real result.
- **A PR**: a title that says what changes, a body with what and why, how it was checked, and screenshots for anything
  visible.

## What you start, you stop
Your run is not over until everything you started is stopped. A server or watcher left running keeps the run open,
holds a port and uses the machine after you are gone.
- Start a server you only need for a while in the background, note its process id, and **stop it before your final
  message** (`kill <pid>`). Example: `python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 &` to look at frames, then `kill %1`
  when the screenshots are taken.
- **Ports**: the board gives each worktree its own (in your prompt); otherwise pick a free one and check it is free
  first. Bind to `127.0.0.1`, not to every interface.
- Temporary files go in your working folder's own scratch place, not in the user's home or `/tmp` of another tool.

## Files
- **Write only inside your working folder** (or the worktree), and outputs a person should see (reports,
  screenshots, logs) in the ticket's Workspace (its path is in your prompt, or `manage_ticket(action='workspace')`). Never edit the person's own config, dotfiles or other projects, and
  never delete what you did not create.
- Do not commit generated files, build output, secrets or large binaries; check `git status` before each commit.
